articles.title: Nostalgia bait and the political economy of time: Future shock in algorithmic culture
articles.authors: Richard Frenneaux
articles.abstract: This study examines how platform capitalism transforms temporal distress into economic value through “nostalgia bait”—algorithmically optimized content that remediates recent cultural artefacts to extract engagement from users experiencing technological acceleration. Integrating Toffler's (1970) concept of future shock with Sharma's (2014) power-chronography, the research demonstrates how platforms incorporate the psychological conditions they claim to address, converting temporal anxiety into a core profit mechanism. Using dual methods—thematic analysis of 5610 TikTok comments and semi-structured interviews with ten music industry professionals—the study traces recursive relationships between user temporal displacement and creator labor constraints. Findings reveal three dynamics of temporal exploitation: (1) platforms commodify psychological responses to acceleration through manufactured nostalgia, with 42% of comments expressing temporal displacement; (2) algorithmic systems restructure creative labor through recommendation dependencies, compelling producers to optimize content around seven-second attention windows and content calendar logic rather than artistic vision; (3) embodied nostalgic affect becomes extractable behavioral data through the standardization of sensory language, including phrases such as “unexplainable chills” and “core memory.” The research advances three theoretical contributions: extending future shock theory to demonstrate how conditions identified in 1970 become engineered features of 21st-century business models; operationalizing power-chronography through empirical analysis of platform temporal architectures; and systematically connecting production and consumption dynamics to reveal self-reinforcing cycles of extraction. The findings carry implications for temporal sovereignty in algorithmic culture and for the development of alternative infrastructures oriented toward human continuity rather than platform profit.

articles.title: Breaking through barriers and shadowbans: How disabled influ-activists navigate algorithmic challenges
articles.authors: Manuela Farinosi, Cabiria Gridelli
articles.abstract: Despite disability’s centrality to digital inclusion debates, scholarship on disabled influencers remains limited, focusing primarily on representation rather than material advocacy conditions. This study examines how disabled influencers navigate platform constraints while pursuing digital advocacy, extending Van Dijk’s access framework to content creation contexts through semi-structured interviews with sixteen Italian content creators on Instagram and TikTok. Digital inclusion emerges not as linear progression but as ongoing negotiation with systematically biased technological and commercial systems. Findings reveal sophisticated adaptive strategies including “algorithmic advocacy literacy” and “experiential pedagogy” that transform lived experience into educational resources. However, these operate within structural constraints including “systematic advocacy suppression” through shadowbanning, automated content removal, and monetization restrictions. The study introduces “accessibility maintenance work,” invisible, uncompensated labour creators perform to make platforms genuinely accessible, while revealing economic stratification where resource availability directly correlates with advocacy capacity. Results challenge approaches privileging technological solutions over systematic reform, demonstrating how platform governance constrains advocacy through accumulated algorithmic bias and automated moderation lacking contextual understanding.

articles.title: Playing with Fire, Losing the Drive: Bidirectional Links Between Problematic Smartphone Use and Grit Dimensions
articles.authors: Luming Zhao, Jiaxi Peng
articles.abstract: This study examined bidirectional longitudinal associations between grit dimensions (consistency of interest [CI] and perseverance of effort [PE]) and problematic smartphone use (PSU) and tested cognitive flexibility as a mediating mechanism. A sample of 1,641 Chinese university students (55.2 percent female; Mage = 20.1 years) completed measures at two time points 6 months apart. A four-variable cross-lagged panel model revealed that CI and PSU negatively predicted each other over time, whereas PSU unidirectionally predicted decreased PE. Cognitive flexibility partially mediated the PSU-to-PE pathway (indirect effect = −0.004, 95 percent bootstrap CI [−0.010, −0.0001]). Competing models analysis confirmed this directionality: the forward mediation (PSU → cognitive flexibility → PE) was significant, whereas the reverse was not. These findings demonstrate that grit dimensions exhibit distinct longitudinal patterns with PSU and identify cognitive flexibility as a cognitive mechanism through which PSU specifically undermines effort persistence. Implications for dimensional approaches to grit and targeted interventions are discussed.

articles.title: Online Social Anxiety in the Digital Age: Transitions, Predictors, and Mental Health Associations in Emerging Adulthood
articles.authors: Ao Liu, Zheng Zhang, Xintian Hong, Rumiao Pan, Zhihao Ma, Yuanyuan Wang
articles.abstract: Background: Online social anxiety (OSA), a multidimensional form of social evaluative anxiety in online social contexts, disproportionately affects emerging adults who constitute the largest active group of media users and face heightened psychological sensitivity due to growing pressures and immature sociocognitive regulation during the transition to adulthood. However, its heterogeneity, transitions, and longitudinal associations with mental health outcomes remain underexplored. Methods: This study utilized data from two waves of a three-wave longitudinal survey, with 849 Chinese participants ( Mean age = 21.6 years; 50.4 percent female) assessed at 4-month intervals. Individuals were classified using latent profile analysis and the stability and changes of profiles were assessed via latent transition analysis (LTA). Multinomial logistic regressions were conducted separately at baseline and follow-up to identify correlates of profile membership. Predictors of profile transitions were examined using manual three-step LTA models, and associations between latent transition patterns and follow-up mental health outcomes were examined using BCH-LTA distal outcome analyses controlling for the corresponding baseline symptom level. Results: Four profiles of OSA were identified: low, privacy-sensitive, moderate-high, and high OSA. Extreme profiles (low/high OSA) showed high stability (80.4 percent and 79.1 percent), while privacy-sensitive OSA exhibited the lowest stability (55.1 percent). Profile memberships were influenced by social-cognitive biases and digital interaction, particularly fear of negative evaluation and online interpersonal trust, whereas profile transitions were mainly associated with anxiety. Transitions toward less severe OSA profiles were generally associated with better subsequent mental health, whereas transitions toward more severe profiles corresponded to poorer outcomes, particularly for offline social anxiety. Conclusion: OSA was heterogeneous in its manifestation, severity and transitions. Personalized and early interventions targeting profile-specific vulnerabilities are critical to prevent the worsening of OSA and mitigate its psychological burden.

articles.title: Trust beyond algorithms: What drives Italian audiences’ perceptions of search results and news produced with AI
articles.authors: Giulia Sbaraini Fontes, Sergio Splendore
articles.abstract: This article examines what drives audiences’ trust levels across different configurations of artificial intelligence (AI) use within the information ecosystem. We rely on a representative survey of Italian adults, performed in September 2025, to analyse trust patterns when (a) AI acts as an intermediary through automated search results and (b) when it is embedded in news organisations. Our findings show that AI-generated search results are more trusted than news, highlighting the growing role of platforms as primary information providers. Moreover, trust in news is positively associated with trust in news produced with AI, regardless of the source, challenging prevailing assumptions of ‘algorithmic aversion’ even in a traditional setting like Italy. These results suggest a shift in the foundations of media trust, with important implications for the role of journalism in an increasingly platform-driven information ecosystem.

articles.title: Examining the relationships between time pressure, challenge and hindrance technostressors and work outcomes in online labour markets
articles.authors: Azka Umair, Eoin Whelan, Kieran Conboy
articles.abstract: Purpose The antecedents and consequences of technostress are well documented. Yet, one aspect of the technostress process that is not well understood is the role of time in shaping perceptions of technostress. This research investigates the relationships between time pressure, technostress and work outcomes in online labour markets (OLMs), a context where work accomplishment is highly dependent upon time. Design/methodology/approach This study uses transactional theory of stress as a theoretical perspective to empirically test a research model explaining the link between time pressure and challenge and hindrance technostressors. Survey data were gathered from 354 workers in a widely used OLM. Structural equation modelling was used to evaluate the research model. Findings The findings show that time pressure plays a dual role, acting as a potential catalyst for both positive and negative effects of technostress in OLMs. Time pressure is significantly related to both challenge and hindrance technostressors. The findings also show that challenge and hindrance technostressors can create a time distortion effect in OLMs. However, despite experiencing hindrance technostressors, the workers in OLMs consider their work important and meaningful. A post-hoc analysis also suggests that the experience of challenge technostressors buffers the negative effect of hindrance technostressors on meaningful work. Originality/value The study extends the prior research by theorising and validating the importance of temporal elements in the technostress process. Time pressure acts as a key environmental antecedent contributing to technostress in OLMs. This study explores how technostressors affect unique work outcomes, such as time distortion and meaningfulness of work in OLMs.

articles.title: How virtual learning communities evolve towards social learning: insights from 204 massive open online courses
articles.authors: Ge Mu, Jie Xiong, Jie Yan, Lu Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose Virtual learning communities (VLCs) are central to large-scale online education. Their interaction patterns affect the quality of social learning, learner engagement and the sustainability of online courses. Most previous studies take a static perspective, showing only snapshots of VLC structures and ignoring how interactions change over time. This study provides a holistic view of VLCs in massive open online courses (MOOCs), focusing on their dynamic evolution and the conditions that make them more supportive of social learning. Design/methodology/approach Guided by social learning theory, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of 204 VLCs and 4,385 sequential networks from MOOC forums. Findings Our social network analysis first identifies the main structural characteristics of MOOC forum networks, then categorizes them into eight distinct types using three key quantitative indicators and finally maps out the potential evolutionary paths these communities follow as they transition between adjacent structural categories (changing one indicator) or across multiple categories (changing two or more indicators over time). Many MOOC communities show low centralization, a high proportion of isolates and low connection density. These patterns are not conducive to social learning. However, certain paths enable their transformation into structures better suited for it. Originality/value To the best of our knowledge, this study is among the first to systematically classify VLC network structures in MOOCs and examine their temporal evolution using sequential network analysis. It shows how communities shift between configurations and identifies the pathways that lead towards more effective social learning.

articles.title: Creating mental imagery of cultural creative product with AR: a mixed-methods study of the affordances and consumer responses
articles.authors: Bin Li, Zhou Qi
articles.abstract: Purpose Cultural and creative products is embracing augmented reality (AR) as a new opportunity to explain traditional culture and revitalize heritage marketing. However, effects and psychological mechanisms of this intersection remain underexplored. This study draws upon affordance perspective and develops a conceptual framework based on mental imagery theory, aiming to elucidate affordances and consumer responses of AR cultural creative products through a mixed-methods design. Design/methodology/approach Firstly, this study investigates affordances of AR (i.e. aesthetics, functionality, symbolism, interactivity and symbiosis) that enables cultural representation through interviews. Subsequently, a cross-sectional survey demonstrates the performance of AR. Findings The affordances of AR (i.e. aesthetics, functionality, symbolism, interactivity and symbiosis) help consumers to build mental imagery (i.e. elaboration and quality) of the culture and psychological proximity, contributing to positive outcome (i.e. consumer satisfaction, purchase intention and cultural identification). Originality/value These findings offer insights into AR research and provide practical guidance on how to deploy AR for cultural and creative products.

articles.title: Placing the 5G bets in the early stage: the influence of 5G strategy implementation on credit rating
articles.authors: Xin Bao, Lu Lu, Baiqing Sun, Raymond Lau
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of fifth generation mobile communication technology (5G) strategy implementation on credit ratings and to test the moderating effects of firm attributes on the focal association in the early stage of 5G business application. Design/methodology/approach The research utilized a sample of 573 unique S&P 1500 firms in the early implementation stage of 5G from 2015 to 2020. We then tested the hypotheses with the ordinal logit model. Findings The findings reveal that early-stage 5G strategy implementation negatively impacts credit ratings by increasing default risk and lowering firm value. However, this negative relationship is weakened for firms with higher cash ratios, greater slack, lower capital intensity, and for firms in high-growth industries or with 5G patents. Additionally, firms with 5G strategy implementation face higher bond yields compared to their counterparts. Practical implications This study provides an in-depth understanding of the impact of early-stage 5G strategy implementation on credit ratings for firm managers and capital market participants. Findings help managers navigate early-stage 5G credit constraints, while creditors price these risky strategies based on firm financial attributes. Originality/value This is likely to be the first study that explores the challenges of 5G strategy implementation for credit constraints. The findings of this study reveal that implementing 5G strategies in the early stage tends to signal higher risk-taking incentives. In particular, it highlights resource dependence factors that mitigate the negative impact of 5G strategy implementation on credit ratings.

articles.title: Who to activate next? Predicting influential and susceptible users in social media marketing with CFT-SIS
articles.authors: Syrios Siyao Li, Sufang Wang, Yufei Wu, Yuanyuan Jamie Li, Matthew Kwok On Lee
articles.abstract: Purpose The proliferation of online social networks (OSNs) has brought opportunities and challenges in managing marketing information flows. This study aims to develop an organization-level personalized monitoring model for marketing campaigns, which not only tracks the dynamics of information dissemination but also identifies influential, susceptible and cost-efficient participants to activate in the next round of campaigns. Design/methodology/approach This study develops a novel CFT-SIS framework that integrates curated flows theory (CFT) with the epidemiological susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) framework and differentiates information dissemination through broadcasting and narrowcasting channels. It combines users’ susceptibility with their historical influence in brand-specific campaigns to construct the influence-susceptibility index (ISI), precisely measuring both activation difficulty and resulting impact. Findings The CFT-SIS framework enables real-time monitoring of information diffusion by capturing both horizontal spread within individual campaigns and longitudinal interconnections across multiple campaigns. Compared to conventional SIS formulations, it demonstrates higher accuracy and stability in predicting user states. The proposed ISI effectively identifies dual-role users who are both highly influential and easily activated, enabling deeper propagation at lower cost and highlighting participants who drive sustained campaign success. Originality/value This study advances theoretical understanding of sustained social media marketing by identifying a novel and structurally emergent mechanism through which curation hierarchy reshapes user susceptibility and influence across network positions over time. In practice, the model enables the identification of high-impact, easily activated users, supporting more efficient campaign design and resource allocation in social media marketing.

articles.title: “Communicating in the Air Force”: the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication , and U.S. military education, 1950–1962
articles.authors: Dominique Trudel, David W Park
articles.abstract: This article explores the intertwined history of the National Society for the Study of Communication (NSSC), its Journal of Communication, and U.S. Air Force educational programs. Founded in 1950 (and renamed the International Communication Association in 1969), NSSC developed a close partnership with the Air Force’s Air University in its early days. The growth of the academic society and the expansion of communication courses in military education programs were then mutually reinforcing: NSSC leaders—including several Air Force officers and civilian consultants—helped define and refine military communication curricula. Air University resources supported NSSC projects, most notably the Journal of Communication. Drawing on extensive archival research and a close reading of the Journal’s content during its first decade, this article argues that these collaborations not only nurtured NSSC’s institutional development, but also shaped a specific conception of communication emphasizing vocational training, efficiency, and the transmission of command.

articles.title: Through their eyes: neural and behavioral evidence for enhanced immersion via point-of-view editing
articles.authors: Moran Ovadia, Shiri Davidovitch, Romi Sion, Naama Shoham, Nimrod Keren, Sergei Freedman, Cynthia Cabañas, Dov Rubinstein, Mark A Thornton, Jonathan Frome, Liad Mudrik, Tim J Smith, Gal Raz
articles.abstract: Point-of-view (POV) editing—the juxtaposition of a character’s gaze with the object of that gaze—is presumed to function as a unique empathic device that dissolves viewer-character boundaries; however, direct empirical evidence remains scarce. This study provides the first systematic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral investigation into whether POV editing facilitates shared attention and intentionality. 39 adults viewed 8 original narrative movies containing POV sequences or closely matched control conditions. POV sequences increased fixation durations on characters’ faces and enhanced subsequent recognition of gazed-at content. Neurally, POV editing elicited stronger responses in regions implicated in mentalizing and increased shared, item-specific activation patterns across viewers within areas associated with perspective-taking and goal-directed control. Multivariate decoding further indicates that a character’s gaze induced more robust neural signatures of character identity on subsequent target elements. Together, these findings support a functional role for POV editing in promoting joint attention and shared intentionality in audiovisual messages.

articles.title: When YouTube-Specific Content Feels Positive
articles.authors: Min Jung Kim, Drew P. Cingel
articles.abstract: Abstract: This paper examines the prospective associations among positive verbal and physical expressions in YouTube-specific content, children's parasocial relationships, the quality of their offline peer relationships, and parents' perceptions of YouTube's role in child development. We conducted a three-wave longitudinal survey combined with a content analysis of 97 parents with children aged four to 6. Using structural equation modeling (SEM), we found that positive verbal and physical expressions in YouTube-specific content at Year 1 were significantly associated with children's parasocial relationships at Year 2. Parasocial relationships at Year 2 were negatively associated with the quality of children’s offline peer relationships at Year 3 but positively associated with parents’ perceptions of YouTube in the same year. By linking expressive features in YouTube-specific content to children's parasocial relationships and subsequent peer relationship quality and parental perceptions, the findings provide insight into how media environments may shape early social development.

articles.title: Young Adult Siblings’ Management of Parental Differential Treatment: An Integrative Framework of Uncertainty and Attachment
articles.authors: Weimiao Zhou, Alesia Woszidlo
articles.abstract: Drawing upon uncertainty management and attachment theories, this study examines how young adult siblings manage parental differential treatment (PDT) through avoidance or information seeking, and how these communication strategies are shaped by situational factors of fairness appraisals and emotional responses as well as by the relational schema of parent-child attachment. Using quantitative survey data and open-ended written accounts from 405 young adults who recalled an episode of differential parental support between themselves and their target siblings, we identified four distinct communication strategies: adaptive avoidance, fearful avoidance, self-initiated information seeking, and parent-initiated information seeking. Multinomial logistic regression results suggested that fairness appraisals predicted the likelihood of different emotional responses (i.e., positive, negative, or neutral/mixed emotions). Testing both situational and relational schema predictors, results further indicated that lower levels of fairness appraisals, negative emotions, and less parental attachment were generally associated with increased odds of young adult siblings’ using fearful avoidance strategy and decreased odds of their using adaptive avoidance or parent-initiated information seeking strategies. Implications for fostering children’s effective cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses in managing PDT are discussed.

articles.title: The Way We Were(n’t): Insecurity Bias in Memories of Adult Attachment Relationships
articles.authors: Maggie C. Palmiero, R. Chris Fraley
articles.abstract: When people think about their former romantic relationships, they often recall themselves as having been insecure in those relationships. It is possible that those former relationships were, in fact, insecure. But it is also possible that people have a bias to see former relationships in a way that is more insecure than might be warranted. To evaluate these possibilities, in Study 1 we first demonstrated that people do, in fact, consider themselves more insecure in former versus current relationships. In Study 2 we analyzed prospective data from people who eventually would experience a breakup but had not yet. We found that their relationships were more insecure than relationships that did not end, suggesting that part of the difference is due to differences in insecurity while relationships were ongoing. In Study 3, we found that retrospective reports of former relationships were higher in attachment avoidance than should be expected based on prospective data on insecurity. Taken together, these findings suggest that people likely have a bias to see their former relationships as more avoidant than is warranted.

articles.title: Loving Through Pain and Devotion: A Psychobiographical Study of Love in the Life of Müslüm Gürses
articles.authors: Ömer Gökhan Ulum
articles.abstract: This study examines the evolution of love and relational attachment in the life of Müslüm Gürses (1953–2013), a seminal figure in Turkish popular culture whose biography offers a profound lens into the intersection of personal trauma and devotion. Grounded exclusively in Object Relations Theory, the research explores how Gürses’ early experiences of fragmented primary relationships and maternal/paternal loss shaped his subsequent psychological conceptualization of love, both in his private life and his public persona as “Müslüm Baba” (Father Müslüm). Adopting a qualitative psychobiographical design, the study utilizes a comprehensive analysis of biographical materials and developmental milestones, supplemented by the thematic analysis of his core song lyrics. The findings reveal that love in Gürses’ life operated not merely as a romantic pursuit but as a “reparative” and “compensatory” mechanism driven by object-seeking. Through this psychic lens, the analysis demonstrates how Gürses functioned as a stable, containing object for his audience, transforming personal relational trauma into a collective, devotion-based love characterized by mutual emotional containment. By focusing strictly on the psychobiographical development of love amid adversity, this study illustrates how an individual’s internal object world can bridge personal trauma and universal devotion, offering distinct insights into the dynamics of love and personality within specific cultural contexts.

articles.title: The Meanings of News: How U.S. Adults Think About the Word “News”
articles.authors: Stephanie Edgerly, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Christopher M. Dobmeier, Nathan Walter
articles.abstract: This study explores the immediate, top-of-mind meanings audiences hold about “news.” Inspired by recent audience-centric approaches in defining news, we adopt a schema framework to investigate mental representations of the news concept. Using a national probability survey of U.S. adults, we employ a thought-listing exercise combined with a network analysis. Our findings paint a complex picture of news and its meaning today. We identify six distinct news schemas (i.e., clusters of co-occurring words) that correspond to different audience demographics, political ideology, and news consumption. The findings underscore that news is a dynamic concept with implications for journalism scholarship and practice.

articles.title: The Hollowing Out of Nonprofit News: An Ethnographic Investigation into the Implications of Exploited News Workers
articles.authors: Jocelyn McKinnon-Crowley
articles.abstract: This work examines the practices of news workers within the unique funding structures of nonprofit news organizations using qualitative interviews and ethnographic methods. From a political economy perspective, my findings show that organizational concerns are prioritized over journalism by news workers in nonprofit news contexts. I argue this exploits public-service oriented journalists to do unpaid labor. I suggest that dependence on external funders reduces the power of nonprofit news organizations to do journalism.

articles.title: “AI’s Good, but People Have Hearts”: Artificial Intelligence in Data-Driven Journalism in Ghanaian Newsrooms
articles.authors: Theodora Dame Adjin-Tettey, Samuel Danso
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers tremendous potential to advance data journalism by empowering journalists to analyse massive datasets and produce insights for investigative reporting. Through the lens of the technology acceptance model and the social construction of technology theory, this study employed qualitative methods to investigate how Ghanaian journalists adopt AI tools in data journalism. The findings indicate that AI tools are primarily used to support research, idea generation, editing, story development, and visual data representation. Journalists also perceive AI as enhancing efficiency, accessibility, and storytelling capacity. These perceptions align with the perceived usefulness dimension of the technology acceptance model as AI is viewed as improving productivity and strengthening audience engagement and trust. However, several challenges, including high subscription costs, limited availability of context-specific datasets, and persistent ethical concerns, hinder the adoption of AI technologies in data journalism. We argue that these challenges highlight the social context within which technology is adopted, which the social construction of technology theory accounts for.

articles.title: The role of AI competencies: How do AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes shape users’ understanding and evaluation of explainable news recommendations?
articles.authors: Chenyue Wang, Anne C. Kroon, Judith Möller, Claes H. de Vreese, Sophie C. Boerman
articles.abstract: This study investigates how explanations in AI-driven news recommender systems (RS) influence user understanding, trust, and attitudes toward the RS, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in AI competence. An online experiment ( N = 754) was conducted in the Netherlands with a no-explanation condition as baseline. Results show that joint explanations significantly improved users’ objective understanding of the RS but had no consistent direct effects on perceived understanding, trust, or attitudes toward the RS. Exploratory structural equation modeling revealed an indirect pathway in which explanations enhanced objective understanding, which increased perceived understanding, subsequently fostering greater trust and more positive attitudes. Moderation analyses showed limited evidence for AI competence conditioning explanation effects, with small benefits concentrated among users with higher AI knowledge. Together, these findings suggest that explanations in news RS are not universally effective: their effects appear to operate primarily through cognitive mechanisms, while competence-related differences remain limited and selective.

articles.title: Algorithmic muteness: How algorithmic management obstructs platform content operators’ resonance with their labor
articles.authors: Zhenyu Qiu, Jinfeng Du, Irina Y. Yu, Jiankun Gong, Yu Zuo
articles.abstract: Workers who plan, curate, and promote content fuel platforms’ traffic success, yet frequently experience their labor as leaving no meaningful trace. While critical scholarship links this estrangement to algorithmic management, how it reshapes the quality of workers’ relationship with their own labor remains underexplored. Drawing on Rosa’s Resonance Theory and 27 interviews with platform content operators at China’s leading internet companies, this study reveals how algorithmic management obstructs resonance across content production, distribution, and feedback. Quantification hollows out labor’s normative worth; black-boxing forecloses self-efficacy through the (un)controllability paradox; amplification and acceleration suspend the possibility of self-transformation, even amid measurable success. We conceptualize ‘algorithmic muteness’, which captures a relational state—workers maintain high-intensity, data-mediated contact with their labor, yet this contact rarely yields genuine responsiveness. Algorithmic muteness moves beyond documenting the static, structural consequences of algorithmic management (e.g. alienation, meaninglessness) to tracing the relational process producing them, while critically revealing algorithms’ deep entanglement with platform capital.

articles.title: Anxiety, Depression, and Friendship: Friends Don't Run From Trouble
articles.authors: Sarah Knapp‐Loker, Lisa Walsh, Anthony Rodriguez, Victor Kaufman
articles.abstract: Social connectedness—an issue important to individuals, researchers, and clinicians—has been increasingly included in public policy as an antidote to ill‐being. Social connection can be gained through friendships; however, not all friendships are alike, and some may be better suited for accommodating mental health challenges. Thus, the impact of disorders such as anxiety and depression may differentially relate to satisfaction with different types of friendships. In the current study ( N = 1627), adults self‐reported anxiety, depression, psychological variables of interest, and satisfaction with three different types of friendships: intimacy with a best friend, closeness within their network of friends, and socializing within their network of friends. We systematically tested the effects of anxiety and depression separately, additively, interactively, and nonlinearly on the three different friendship dimensions, after controlling for psychological variables that may also contribute to the association. Our hypotheses stating that anxiety and depression would predict greater friendship quality as varied by the level of intimacy characterized within each friendship dimension were supported. This research suggests that the most intimate relationships with best friends may be particularly well‐suited for weathering challenges.

articles.title: When academic leaders disconnect from social media in Finland: Situational rationality, silent resistance
articles.authors: Leena Ripatti-Torniainen, Karoliina Talvitie-Lamberg
articles.abstract: This qualitative study, conducted at Finland’s research universities, analyses high-profile academic leaders who have chosen to be disconnected from social media. We conducted individual interviews with 19 leaders and performed a situational analysis to investigate the rationale for abstaining from social media. Academic leaders rationalised disconnection by reasons related to personality, sociability, critical rationality, and health and security. The leaders’ intensive involvement in three social worlds intensified the individual rationale for disconnection and enabled the leaders to work successfully despite disconnection. These social worlds were research and science, sensitive academia, and insider networks in society. In the context of the managerial neoliberal university, its promotional communication culture, and competition for visibility, the leaders’ disconnection from social media has a dissident, resistant characteristic. The study contributes to prior research through its comprehensive approach to academic leaders’ operational environment. Future research should elaborate on the systemic approach to social media in universities.

articles.title: From Storytelling to Truth-Telling: Narrative Integrity in Science Communication
articles.authors: Tom van Laer, Anne-Sophie Chaxel
articles.abstract: Science storytelling can make evidence intelligible, memorable, and culturally resonant, yet persuasive narratives may still misrepresent how scientific knowledge is produced. This commentary argues that communicators need a standard beyond narrative trust: narrative integrity. The concept evaluates whether a story preserves science’s uncertainty, multicausality, collective labor, provisional conclusions, and capacity for revision. Drawing on research on transportation, framing, anecdotal bias, and processing fluency, we explain how narrative form can outrun evidence even when individual claims are accurate. We then propose six principles for designing stories that remain engaging while representing scientific inquiry honestly, transparently, and responsibly to diverse public audiences.

articles.title: Accuracy and Defense Motives: Exploring Types of Information Insufficiency in the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) Model
articles.authors: Timothy K. F. Fung, Ho Man Leung, Po Yan Lai, Robert J. Griffin
articles.abstract: This study reconceptualizes information insufficiency as a goal-contingent construct within the Risk Information Seeking and Processing model. In multifaceted risk contexts, individuals confront health threats alongside challenges to deep-seated values and beliefs, producing different judgmental demands within a single risk event. Survey data from 858 Hong Kong adults show two distinct forms of information insufficiency, one oriented toward accurate safety judgments and another toward defending deep-seated values and beliefs. Each form is associated with distinct patterns of information seeking and processing. This study demonstrates how multiple goal-based information insufficiencies operate within the same individual in response to different judgmental demands.

articles.title: When Moral Appeals Backfire and Discourage the Adoption of Plant-Based Meat Alternatives
articles.authors: Yuanke Zhou, Wanjun Li, Liudmila Tarabashkina, Zhiyuan Wang
articles.abstract: Public campaigns use moral appeals to promote a plant-based meat diet, but such appeals can also backfire. We found that the animal welfare appeal prompted higher purchase intention only among individuals with lower meat attachment and was damaging among consumers with higher meat attachment, with meat attachment moderating the pathway from meat-related cognitive dissonance to the adoption of plant-based meat. The best strategy to appeal to consumers with higher meat attachment was a description that did not contain any messages. Our study clarifies when and why moral appeals may backfire when promoting plant-based meat, delineating the limits of their persuasiveness.

articles.title: Revisiting the Communication Mediation Model in the Age of Social Media: Longitudinal Evidence From Climate Misinformation Responses in China
articles.authors: Liang Chen, Xiaoming Liu, Lunrui Fu
articles.abstract: The Communication Mediation Model (CMM) posits that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which shapes attitudes and behaviors. Yet its assumptions of linear sequencing and universal applicability remain underexamined. In the era of social media, communication flows are increasingly reciprocal and socially embedded, and response behaviors such as misinformation correction and fact-checking represent new forms of media engagement rather than merely offline actions. Using a three-wave panel survey in China ( n = 499), this study revises the CMM in the context of climate change misinformation on social media by testing temporal pathways and audience heterogeneity. Results show that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which in turn predicts correction, though these relationships unfold concurrently within a single time interval rather than following a staggered temporal order. Multigroup analysis reveals that public self-consciousness conditions pathway activation. Findings highlight how social media environments extend the behavioral scope of the CMM and complicate its assumed temporal order. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

articles.title: Scaling Down: Notes From the Laundry Room
articles.authors: Jeffrey Fossett
articles.abstract: This essay tells the story of a personal experiment in deploying a “deliberative technology” called Polis to start a conversation about the norms of my apartment building’s shared laundry room—a small, quasi-public space ordinarily governed mostly by unspoken rules. The Polis conversation drew meaningful engagement from neighbors, who both voted on shared norms for the space and suggested concrete (and ultimately effective) ways to improve it. Reflecting on this example, I argue that beyond their familiar promise of “scaling up” deliberation, tools like Polis can also facilitate “scaling down,” making it feasible to convene conversations and build a sense of shared interest even in small-scale, everyday settings like the apartment laundry room.

articles.title: Anthropomorphizing AI: Perceptions, Interpretations, and the Humanization of Generative AI
articles.authors: Mohammad Hossein Jarrahi, Amir Karami, Lisa Park, Ensieh Jarrahi, Christoph Lutz
articles.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly advanced AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, has transformed human–AI interactions by providing unprecedentedly natural interaction environments. These developments have significantly heightened user perceptions of AI as human-like, making anthropomorphism, a tendency to attribute human traits to non-humans, increasingly prevalent. Despite the recognition of the rising anthropomorphism in these interaction modalities, little is known about how people anthropomorphize generative AI, especially in social media discourse. Using Twitter/X as a discursive space, we systematically analyze how users described and engaged with ChatGPT, identifying distinct categories and recurring forms of anthropomorphism. Findings reveal diverse anthropomorphic perceptions, including personification, emotional attributions, cognitive and human-like attributes, social interactions, and human-like personality traits. Building on the observation that social media platforms not only reflect but also actively shape and reinforce anthropomorphic narratives, this study raises important implications for trust, misinformation, user expectations, and human–AI interactions.

articles.title: Unpacking the Relationship Between Algorithmic Literacy and Misinformation: A Multidimensional Approach Using Two Sequential Studies
articles.authors: Teresa Correa, Sebastián Valenzuela, Ingrid Bachmann, Nicolás Tobar Jorquera, Natalia Solís-Valdés, Isabel Pavez
articles.abstract: Digital literacy is often proposed as a remedy for misinformation, yet empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness remains mixed. One reason for these inconsistencies lies in the multidimensional nature of both literacy and misinformation. This article focuses on algorithmic literacy, a distinct and increasingly central form of digital literacy in platform-mediated communication, and examines how its cognitive and behavioral dimensions relate to multiple facets of misinformation engagement. Drawing on two probabilistic survey studies conducted in Chile—a nationally representative face-to-face survey ( N = 1,200) and a random-digit-dial telephone survey of urban adults ( N = 2,265)—we analyze how cognitive (algorithmic awareness and knowledge) and behavioral (strategic actions to navigate algorithmic systems) dimensions of algorithmic literacy relate to perceived misinformation exposure, misinformation sharing, objective and subjective news knowledge, and knowledge miscalibration. Across both studies, a consistent pattern emerges: algorithmic literacy is more strongly associated with cognitive outcomes—especially perceived misinformation exposure and knowledge—than with behavioral outcomes like sharing. Higher algorithmic awareness consistently predicts greater perceived exposure, suggesting heightened recognition, while its link to sharing behavior is less consistent. These studies highlight the relevance of distinguishing cognitive from behavioral dimensions of literacy across different stages of misinformation engagement.

articles.title: “Hearing My People, but Not Seeing My People”: Boundaries of Blackness on TikTok
articles.authors: Kylie Gaines-Herrera
articles.abstract: Social media is a valuable tool that enables Black individuals to contest their racialized experiences and engage in counterpublic discourse. Importantly, this opens up cultural property and closed conversations to out-group visibility and appropriation. With this in mind, I ask: How do Black social media users engage in boundary work on TikTok? I create a typology of boundary enforcement on the platform, identifying nine video subtypes, and analyze each subtype using Critical Technocultural Discourse Analysis. The findings suggest that Black TikTok users employ various discursive strategies to maintain group boundaries. This study explores how new technologies may impact racialized experiences and identity formation.

articles.title: Anti-Elitism Gets the Views: Populist Communication and Popularity on German Political YouTube
articles.authors: Lukas Erhard
articles.abstract: YouTube has become a central venue for political communication, but systematic evidence of how parties employ the platform remains limited. This article examines how German political parties use YouTube and how populist rhetoric shapes engagement. We distinguish between anti-elitism and people-centrism and analyze their prevalence in party videos alongside their effects on video performance. We compile a dataset of official YouTube channels from all major German parties (2017–2025), apply automated transcription, and use a transformer-based model (PopBERT) to detect populist language. Video performance is assessed primarily through views, modeled with quantile regression and hurdle approaches to capture the likelihood of videos reaching the top tier and conditional effects among successful content. Our results show that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) far surpasses other parties in subscribers, video production, and engagement. Content analysis reveals that AfD channels contain markedly higher levels of anti-elitist rhetoric, while people-centrism appears more evenly distributed across the party spectrum. Quantile regression models show that anti-elitism is positively associated with engagement in the upper tail of the view distribution for all parties except the Free Democratic Party (FDP). Hurdle models further indicate that anti-elitism is associated with a higher probability of entering the top performance tier not only for the AfD but also for the Christian Democratic Union / Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), Left, and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Results for people-centrism are weaker and less consistent. The study contributes to research on digital populism by showing that anti-elitist rhetoric, more than people-centrism, is associated with video success on YouTube across populist and nonpopulist parties.
